behavior_items: The reproducer defines a minimal SFINAE utility: enable_if<true> contains a nested type alias, while the primary template does not. The alias template enable_if_t<B> therefore becomes valid only when B is true, and otherwise causes substitution failure when used in a dependent context.

Two unrelated types, tuple and pair, are introduced only to create several overload candidates for get. This mimics the standard library situation where many get<N> overloads exist and all may participate in overload resolution.

There are four function templates named get, each taking one of tuple&, const tuple&, pair&, or const pair&, and each returning enable_if_t<N == 1>. This means each overload is only viable when its non-type template argument N is exactly 1; otherwise the return type substitution fails and the overload is removed by SFINAE.

The helper function template frob<N>() is declared constexpr and returns unsigned. Its purpose is to transform an int template parameter into an unsigned non-type template argument while also validating the value.

Inside frob, static_assert(N == 1, "user-friendly diagnostic") intentionally produces a direct diagnostic when N is not 1. This is meant to provide a clear primary error instead of a complicated overload-resolution failure later.

The return statement in frob uses list-initialization: return unsigned{N};. For N = -1 this triggers narrowing diagnostics, because converting the negative int constant -1 to unsigned via braced initialization is ill-formed in a constant-evaluated context.

As a result, frob<-1>() is not a usable constant expression. The compiler reports the failed static_assert, the narrowing conversion, and then notes that the constexpr function body is not valid as a constexpr return path.

The template get_n<N>(tuple& t) performs the key operation: get<frob<N>()>(t). Here frob<N>() is used as a non-type template argument, so the language requires it to be a valid constant expression of the target unsigned type.
In main, get_n<-1>(t) instantiates get_n with N = -1. That forces formation of the expression get<frob<-1>()>(t), which in turn requires immediate constant evaluation of frob<-1>().

The first stage of compiler behavior is therefore instantiation and checking of frob<-1>(). GCC correctly diagnoses that frob<-1>() cannot be used as a constant expression because its static_assert fails and its return statement performs an invalid narrowing conversion.

After that failure, GCC still proceeds into overload resolution for the call to get<frob<-1>()>(t). This is the behavior the bug report objects to: once the explicit template argument expression is already known invalid, continuing to test every overload yields redundant diagnostics.

Each get overload is considered separately as a candidate with an explicit non-type template argument that should match template parameter unsigned N. For every candidate, GCC attempts substitution using the same invalid template argument expression frob<-1>().

Because the invalidity lies in the explicit template argument expression itself, not in any overload-specific property, every candidate fails for the same reason: frob<-1>() is not a constant expression usable as an unsigned template argument.

That produces a cascade of nearly identical messages: candidate found, template argument deduction/substitution failed, frob<-1>() called in a constant expression, not usable as constexpr, and so on. The overload set size directly multiplies the number of repeated diagnostics.

The reproducer demonstrates that SFINAE on the return type enable_if_t<N == 1> is not the main issue being exercised. GCC never reaches a meaningful distinction between N == 1 and N != 1 for the candidates, because the explicit template argument expression itself fails before overload-specific filtering can help.

The pair overloads are deliberately inapplicable from an argument-type perspective because the call passes tuple&, but they still appear in the diagnostic stream because name lookup and template candidate formation happen before final viability is determined. Since the explicit template argument is shared across all candidates, they all trigger the same constant-expression failure path.

The const tuple& overload is also listed even though tuple& would bind better to tuple& than to const tuple&, because GCC is reporting all candidate templates examined during overload resolution, not just the best match. The bug is therefore about diagnostic strategy and premature continuation, not about incorrect overload ranking.

The bug report's core complaint is that an invalid explicit template argument should be treated as a hard failure for the whole call expression, rather than being re-diagnosed once per overload candidate. The expression get<frob<N>()>(t) is already malformed before overload comparison becomes useful.

The report also notes that even if the static_assert-related behavior changes due to another bug fix, the same diagnostic quality issue remains. Removing the static_assert still leaves frob<-1>() non-constant because of the narrowing conversion, and GCC would still emit a wall of repeated overload-resolution errors.

Semantically, the reproducer exercises the interaction between constexpr evaluation, non-type template arguments, explicit function template arguments, SFINAE-constrained overloads, and overload resolution diagnostics. The code is small, but it targets a compiler path where one invalid constant-expression template argument is repeatedly reprocessed for each overload in the candidate set.
test_behavior_analysis.summary: The reproducer builds several SFINAE-constrained get<N> overloads and then calls get<frob<-1>()>(t), where frob<-1>() must be evaluated as a constant expression to form the explicit unsigned non-type template argument. That evaluation fails because frob<-1>() triggers a failing static_assert and an invalid narrowing conversion in return unsigned{N}. GCC correctly diagnoses frob<-1>() as unusable in a constant expression, but then incorrectly continues full overload resolution and re-emits the same template-argument failure for every get overload candidate. The test therefore exercises a diagnostic bug: the call expression is already invalid due to one bad explicit template argument, yet GCC produces a redundant cascade of overload/substitution errors instead of stopping after the primary constant-evaluation failure.

test_failure_analysis.analysis: The common pattern is that a single invalid explicit non-type template argument expression, frob<N>(), is shared by every overload candidate in a function template call. In the reproducer, get<frob<-1>()>(t) requires immediate constant-evaluation of frob<-1>() before overload resolution can meaningfully distinguish among get overloads. GCC correctly detects that frob<-1>() is not a valid constant expression because instantiating the constexpr function triggers a failing static_assert and an ill-formed narrowing conversion in return unsigned{N}. However, after this primary failure, GCC still enters candidate-by-candidate overload resolution and template substitution, re-checking the same already-invalid explicit template argument for each get overload. That indicates the bug is not in SFINAE itself, nor in overload ranking, but in diagnostic control flow around template argument checking: the compiler is failing to treat the malformed explicit template argument as a hard error for the whole call expression and instead propagates it through all overload candidates, producing redundant diagnostics. The likely defect area is GCC front-end code that handles explicit function template arguments, constant-expression validation for non-type template arguments, and suppression/short-circuiting of repeated substitution diagnostics during overload resolution.
possible_causes: Missing short-circuit in function template call processing after an explicit non-type template argument expression has already been diagnosed as non-constant or otherwise invalid.
Incorrect classification of invalid explicit template arguments as candidate-specific substitution failures instead of a call-wide hard error, causing every overload candidate to be retried.
Defect in constexpr/non-type template argument validation path where the result of failed constant evaluation is not cached or propagated, so the same frob<-1>() check is repeated for each overload.
Bug in overload resolution diagnostic machinery that does not suppress duplicate errors when all candidates fail for the same pre-existing template argument expression.

Front-end issue in template argument conversion/checking for explicit function template arguments of unsigned non-type parameter type, especially when the source expression is an invalid constexpr due to narrowing/static_assert failure.

Improper interaction between candidate formation and template argument substitution: overload resolution continues even though template-id formation for get<frob<N>()> should already have failed before overload-specific viability checks.
Diagnostic emission bug in dependent expression handling, where notes about constexpr unusability are attached per candidate rather than once at the point the explicit template argument is formed.
evidence: All reported get overloads fail for the identical reason: frob<-1>() is not usable as a constant expression for template argument unsigned N.
The invalidity is independent of overload parameter types or enable_if conditions, showing the root failure occurs before overload-specific SFINAE or ranking matters.

GCC first emits the primary frob<-1>() diagnostics (static_assert failure, narrowing conversion, constexpr unusable) and only afterward emits repeated candidate substitution errors, indicating lack of early termination.

The pair overloads also participate in the redundant diagnostics even though the function argument is tuple&, which shows the repeated failure happens during generic candidate processing rather than meaningful final viability selection.

The bug report explicitly states that removing static_assert still leaves the same wall of errors due to failed constant evaluation, so the core issue is repeated handling of one invalid NTTP expression, not the particular assertion.

The call syntax uses an explicit template argument expression get<frob<N>()>(t); such expressions must be valid before overload resolution can profitably distinguish candidates, so continuing candidate-by-candidate retries strongly suggests a front-end control-flow/diagnostic bug.

This method adds each overload in the set to the candidate list and threads EXPLICIT_TARGS through overload resolution. Since GCC keeps retrying the same bad template argument for every get overload, the control flow that iterates over overloads and decides whether to continue after a hard template-argument error is highly suspect here.

The bug is specifically that GCC keeps trying every get overload even after the explicit non-type template argument expression frob<-1>() is already invalid. That makes the overload-candidate selection/control-flow here highly suspicious, especially if it treats the bad explicit template argument as a per-candidate substitution issue instead of a call-wide hard failure.
